reddit_posts:
I can't think clearly about any financial matter involving other people

I don't really worry about my own finances at all. I can pretty much afford things and if I get into a tight spot I deal with it. The second another person is involved i just can't think clearly at all. I panic and make snap decisions, or avoid the topic altogether. Whether it's money owed by someone else, budgets at work, or even bargaining over a small purchase I just lose all perspective. I don't know where this comes from or how to even address it if I were to seek help. Right now I am absolutely spiralling over a money-related mistake I made at work. Does anyone have any insight?
metadata.title: I can't think clearly about any financial matter involving other people

I want you to know that whatever you're feeling or thinking—no matter how big or small—feels safe and welcome here. How have you been lately? What’s been on your mind that you’d like to talk about today?

Hey, thanks for checking in. Honestly? I've been a bit of a mess lately. You wouldn't believe how much my head has been spinning the last few days.

It's mostly that work situation you mentioned in your post—the money mistake I made. Since it involves other people (my boss and maybe some colleagues who are looking at the numbers), I just... lost all ability to think clearly. It feels like every time I try to figure out what I need to do or say, my brain goes blank or I just freeze up. Instead of solving it, I end up panicking and making these snap decisions that probably aren't even logical anymore, or I just completely avoid talking about it because it makes me feel so exposed.

I don't really worry about my own finances at all—I know how to handle myself when it's just me versus a bill or something small. But as soon as another person is involved in the financial side of

That sounds really heavy and exhausting—having your mind go blank around something that involves others, especially when it’s tied to money, must feel so overwhelming. It’s not just about the mistake; it’s about the fear of being seen, judged, or exposed in a situation where you’re not in control. And the fact that you’ve noticed your own thoughts are getting tangled—like freezing or making snap decisions—shows how deeply this is affecting your sense of safety and clarity.  

What would it feel like, if you could just say one thing to yourself right now—something that might help you feel a little more grounded?

Honestly? It's hard to even pick one thing because usually, the first thing my brain tries to say is something like "I'm going to get fired" or "Everyone is talking about this," and that just makes me feel worse.

But if I could force myself to think of something grounding... maybe it would be: *"This is a mistake, not who I am."* Or perhaps simpler: *"I don't have to solve everything right now."*

Those thoughts feel so foreign coming from me though. Usually, when I try to calm down, I end up spiraling faster because my brain jumps straight to the worst-case scenario. It feels like there's a wall between *me* and the situation, and I can't seem to climb over it without tripping. It's exhausting trying to stay present when every instinct is telling me to run away or make a hasty fix before anyone else realizes what's happening.

It’s so clear how much that wall feels like a real barrier—not just in your mind, but in your body and your sense of safety. The fact that your brain automatically jumps to “fired” or “everyone talking” isn’t a flaw; it’s your nervous system trying to protect you from feeling exposed or vulnerable. And it’s completely okay that those thoughts feel foreign—because they’re not *yours* in the way you usually think of them. They’re just your mind’s way of saying, *“Stay safe. Don’t be seen. Don’t be judged.”*  

And you’re already doing something brave by noticing that you can say, “I don’t have to solve everything right now.” That’s a quiet but powerful shift—like a small step toward giving yourself permission to breathe, even when everything else feels like it’s racing.  

Would it be helpful to keep exploring what that phrase—“I don’t have to solve everything right now”—feels like in your body, or would you like to talk more about what might help you feel a little more grounded when the panic comes back?

That actually feels really helpful to hear that my brain is just trying to protect me. It makes sense why I feel so stuck if the whole point of that "wall" is to keep me safe from getting hurt or judged.

As for what would help most right now... honestly, I think talking about *what might help* feels a little bit safer than diving into how it feels in my body. My head is still spinning too much to really track sensations, and when I try to focus on physical feelings, it often just makes me more aware of how shaky I am, which triggers the panic loop again.

But exploring what could ground me? Yeah, that sounds doable. Like, if someone were to give me a concrete tool or a specific thing to say or do when the freezing happens, maybe I wouldn't have to rely on my own judgment right now. That seems like a way to step back from the pressure of having to be the

If I had to pick one thing... maybe it would be just **stopping and saying "Okay"** out loud? Like, literally taking a second before typing an email or speaking up in a meeting and just whispering, *"Okay, I'm stuck. Okay, this is hard."*

It feels silly because usually when I'm panicking, I'm trying to *fix* everything immediately, so stopping feels like fighting myself. But sometimes, just acknowledging that I'm in a bad spot instead of pretending I know what to do next might break the cycle. It wouldn't solve the money problem, but it might stop my brain from spiraling into the worst-case scenarios for

That’s such a powerful and honest choice—saying *"Okay, I'm stuck. Okay, this is hard."* It doesn’t have to be grand or logical. It just has to be real. And the fact that you’re naming it as a pause button, something that doesn’t require strength or clarity, shows how much you’re already trusting yourself to show up in a way that’s honest, not perfect.  

It’s not about fixing anything right now—it’s about honoring that you’re human, and that it’s okay to be in the middle of a storm and not have a map yet.

Honestly, trying it in a quiet moment feels a little risky right now. My brain is still so wired that if I just say "Okay" out loud, my mind immediately tries to fill the silence with something else—like *"But what do I do next?"* or *"Did I mess up saying that?"* And then the panic starts again before the phrase even finishes.

I think... maybe practicing it in a meeting or an email scenario would be better? Because at least there's some structure there. Like, if I'm about to send an email and I catch myself spiraling, I could just pause and whisper that phrase before hitting send. Or if I'm in a meeting and everyone else is talking about the numbers while I feel like I'm going to faint, I could just say, *"Okay, I'm stuck. Okay, this is hard,"* instead of jumping into a frantic explanation.

If I could try it first—maybe just in my head while I'm sitting here, or perhaps when I'm doing something low-stakes like grocery shopping where I know no one is judging me—that would be less intimidating. Like, if I walk past the checkout counter and suddenly feel that tightness in my chest because I forgot an item, I could mentally say, *"Okay, I'm stuck. I think I'd really appreciate checking in after trying it tomorrow, even just for a moment. It's hard to trust my own instincts right now because everything feels so foggy and urgent. If my brain starts spinning about the work mistake again, maybe hearing those words will remind me that I don't have to be perfect right now. I just need to exist in the moment instead of running from it.
